title: Workers' compensation: Michigan law, the policy and premium
summary: Follow Tony's Pizza through one slippery Friday: who must carry comp, what it covers and pays, three federal acts, the policy and the premium.
objectives: Explain the exclusive remedy and which Michigan employers must carry comp
Tell covered from uncovered injuries; know the waiting period and 80% benefit
Match the federal acts to the right workers and name the policy's six parts
Compute WC premium from payroll, rate and experience mod

scenes.title: Tony's Pizza and the slippery Friday
scenes.subtitle: Michigan's comp act, three federal acts, the six-part policy and the premium (WC 00 00 00 C, Ed. 1-15)

beats.text: Rewind to before Tony hired drivers and others. Friday night at Tony's Pizza in Detroit: Marco and Lily sling dough, and the floor's getting slippery.
beats.say: Rewind to before Tony hired drivers and others. Friday night at Tony's Pizza in Detroit: Marco and Lily sling dough, and the floor's getting slippery.

beats.text: Workers' comp is 5% of your exam, about 8 questions.
beats.say: Workers' comp is five percent of your exam, about eight questions.

scenes.title: Does Tony have to carry comp?
scenes.hook: 3 at once, or 1 at 35 for 13 (out of the last 52). Public employers: every one, any size.
items: 3 at once: private non-farm employers regularly employing 3 or more at one time
1 at 35 for 13: fewer than 3, but 1 works 35+ hours a week for 13+ of the last 52 weeks
Public employers: all of them, regardless of the number of employees
Farms, household workers: own rules. A voluntary comp endorsement can cover workers not required

beats.text: Dana, it's just me and two cooks. Do I really need comp?
beats.say: Dana, it's just me and two cooks. Do I really need comp?

beats.text: Tony, in Michigan it's 3 at once, or 1 at 35 for 13, out of the last 52. Public employers: every one, any size.
beats.say: Tony, in Michigan it's three at once, or one at thirty-five for thirteen, out of the last fifty-two. Public employers: every one, any size.

beats.text: 3 at once means a private, non-farm employer regularly employing 3 or more at the same time. Fewer than 3? One worker at 35 hours or more a week, for 13 weeks or more of the last 52, is enough. Public employers? All of them, regardless of the number of employees.
beats.say: Three at once means a private, non-farm employer regularly employing three or more at the same time. Fewer than three? One worker at thirty-five hours or more a week, for thirteen weeks or more of the last fifty-two, is enough. Public employers? All of them, regardless of the number of employees.

beats.text: Farms and household workers have their own rules. Watch out: payroll size doesn't decide it. And a voluntary comp endorsement can cover workers the law doesn't require an employer to cover.
beats.say: Farms and household workers have their own rules. Watch out: payroll size doesn't decide it. And a voluntary comp endorsement can cover workers the law doesn't require an employer to cover.

beats.text: Marco has worked 40 hours a week for the last 20 weeks. What does Tony do?
beats.say: Marco has worked forty hours a week for the last twenty weeks. What does Tony do?

options.label: Skip it. I only have two cooks!
options.fail: Fewer than 3 still counts if 1 works 35+ hours a week for 13+ of the last 52 weeks. Marco does.

beats.text: Marco's hours bring Tony under the act. Going uninsured is a misdemeanor, and an injured worker can sue.
beats.say: Marco's hours bring Tony under the act. Going uninsured is a misdemeanor, and an injured worker can sue.

options.label: Have the cooks sign waivers
options.fail: In Michigan, an employee's agreement to waive comp isn't valid. The only exception is certain elections made after an injury.

beats.text: Marco signs a napkin. Worthless: in Michigan, waiving comp up front isn't valid.
beats.say: Marco signs a napkin. Worthless: in Michigan, waiving comp up front isn't valid.

options.label: Pay any claims out of the cash register
options.fail: Comp must be secured: insure with an authorized insurer, or prove solvency and get the state comp agency's okay to self-insure.

beats.text: Paying claims from the register, with no state okay, doesn't secure comp. Tony is uninsured.
beats.say: Paying claims from the register, with no state okay, doesn't secure comp. Tony is uninsured.

options.label: Buy a policy from an authorized insurer
options.win: Insure with an authorized insurer. Can't get coverage normally? The Workers' Compensation Placement Facility: all authorized comp insurers take part.

beats.text: Smart. Dana places Tony with an authorized insurer. Can't get coverage normally? Comp has its own: the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility.
beats.say: Smart. Dana places Tony with an authorized insurer. Can't get coverage normally? Comp has its own: the Michigan Workers' Compensation Placement Facility.

reveal.text: The only other route in Michigan: self-insure, on proof of solvency, with the Workers' Disability Compensation Agency's okay, not DIFS.
reveal.say: The only other route in Michigan: self-insure, on proof of solvency, with the Workers' Disability Compensation Agency's okay, not D I F S.

reveal.text: Two or more employers in one industry with $1,000,000 or more in combined assets may be allowed to self-insure as a group.
reveal.say: Two or more employers in one industry with one million dollars or more in combined assets may be allowed to self-insure as a group.

scenes.title: Friday night: Marco slips
scenes.plain: An injury connected to the job: in the law's words, one arising out of and in the course of employment. No one has to prove fault.
scenes.example: Marco slips on the wet kitchen floor carrying dough. Covered, even though he was rushing, and Tony doesn't have to be at fault.
scenes.exam: On the premises a reasonable time before or after work: presumed in the course of employment. Out: mainly social events, ordinary diseases of life.

beats.text: Crash! Marco slips on the wet kitchen floor with a tray of dough. Is that a compensable injury?
beats.say: Crash! Marco slips on the wet kitchen floor with a tray of dough. Is that a compensable injury?

beats.text: A compensable injury is one connected to the job. In Michigan, comp covers an injury arising out of and in the course of employment. No one has to prove fault, or that Tony was negligent.
beats.say: A compensable injury is one connected to the job. In Michigan, comp covers an injury arising out of and in the course of employment. No one has to prove fault, or that Tony was negligent.

beats.text: Marco was rushing? Still covered. His own carelessness doesn't bar comp; only intentional and willful misconduct would.
beats.say: Marco was rushing? Still covered. His own carelessness doesn't bar comp; only intentional and willful misconduct would.

beats.text: On the premises a reasonable time before or after work, he's presumed to be in the course of employment. Diseases peculiar to the business count too. Out: mainly social events and ordinary diseases of life.
beats.say: On the premises a reasonable time before or after work, he's presumed to be in the course of employment. Diseases peculiar to the business count too. Out: mainly social events and ordinary diseases of life.

items.text: Slips in Tony's kitchen 10 minutes before his shift
items.why: On the premises a reasonable time before work: presumed to be in the course of employment.

items.text: Twists a knee at the staff bowling party
items.why: A mainly social or recreational activity isn't covered, even on the employer's premises.

items.text: Burns his hand on the pizza oven during his shift, rushing
items.why: His own ordinary carelessness doesn't bar comp.

items.text: Catches the cold going around Detroit
items.why: An ordinary disease of life isn't compensable.

items.text: Gets a disease from conditions peculiar to Tony's business
items.why: Conditions characteristic of and peculiar to the business: it counts.

items.text: Hurt by his own intentional, willful misconduct
items.why: The employee's intentional and willful misconduct bars comp.

beats.text: Your turn: which of Marco's mishaps does comp cover?
beats.say: Your turn: which of Marco's mishaps does comp cover?

reveal.text: The test is the work connection, not fault.
reveal.say: The test is the work connection, not fault.

reveal.text: Out: mainly social events, even on the premises, ordinary diseases of life and his own intentional, willful misconduct.
reveal.say: Out: mainly social events, even on the premises, ordinary diseases of life and his own intentional, willful misconduct.

scenes.title: Can Marco sue Tony?
scenes.src: MCL 418.131(1); questions core-054, core-055; adapted from memory hook mn_core-23
scenes.plain: Comp benefits are the worker's only remedy against the employer for a work injury or occupational disease.
scenes.example: A room with one door: for an employer who carries comp, benefits are the only way out. Marco gets benefits, not a lawsuit against Tony.
scenes.exam: One trapdoor: an intentional tort, a deliberate act with specific intent to injure. Even gross negligence is not enough.

beats.text: Marco, sue Tony for a million dollars!
beats.say: Marco, sue Tony for a million dollars!

beats.text: Tony is insured, so in Michigan comp is Marco's exclusive remedy against him: his only remedy for a work injury or occupational disease. Picture a room with one door: benefits are the only way out. Marco gets benefits, not a lawsuit against Tony.
beats.say: Tony is insured, so in Michigan comp is Marco's exclusive remedy against him: his only remedy for a work injury or occupational disease. Picture a room with one door: benefits are the only way out. Marco gets benefits, not a lawsuit against Tony.

beats.text: The one trapdoor is an intentional tort: a deliberate act with specific intent to injure. Intent is also deemed, meaning treated as proven, if the employer knew an injury was certain and willfully disregarded it.
beats.say: The one trapdoor is an intentional tort: a deliberate act with specific intent to injure. Intent is also deemed, meaning treated as proven, if the employer knew an injury was certain and willfully disregarded it.

beats.text: Even gross negligence is not enough.
beats.say: Even gross negligence is not enough.

scenes.title: Marco's call: sue Tony?
scenes.src: MCL 418.131(1); questions core-054, core-055; memory hook mn_core-23

beats.text: Tony knew that floor gets slick, and he never bought a mat!
beats.say: Tony knew that floor gets slick, and he never bought a mat!
beats.speaker: Marco

beats.text: Comp is paying Marco. Now what?
beats.say: Comp is paying Marco. Now what?

options.label: Sue Tony. He was super careless!
options.fail: Even gross negligence isn't an intentional tort. Comp stays Marco's exclusive remedy against Tony.

beats.text: 'Really, really careless' doesn't open the trapdoor. Even gross negligence isn't an intentional tort.
beats.say: 'Really, really careless' doesn't open the trapdoor. Even gross negligence isn't an intentional tort.

draw.text: Gross negligence is not an intentional tort

options.label: Sue Tony. He knew someone might get hurt!
options.fail: Deemed intent needs actual knowledge an injury was certain, plus willful disregard. Possible is not certain.

beats.text: Nope. Knowing an injury was possible isn't knowing it was certain.
beats.say: Nope. Knowing an injury was possible isn't knowing it was certain.

options.label: Take the comp benefits
options.win: Comp is Marco's exclusive remedy against Tony. With no intentional tort, benefits are the one way out.

beats.text: Smart. Marco takes his comp benefits, the one door out. Tony buys a floor mat.
beats.say: Smart. Marco takes his comp benefits, the one door out. Tony buys a floor mat.

reveal.text: Only an intentional tort opens the trapdoor. Even gross negligence doesn't, and knowing an injury was possible isn't knowing it was certain.
reveal.say: Only an intentional tort opens the trapdoor. Even gross negligence doesn't, and knowing an injury was possible isn't knowing it was certain.

scenes.title: Michigan: Marco's waiting period and benefit
scenes.hook: Wait 7, paid from day 8, back-paid at 2 weeks. Then 80% of after-tax wages, capped at 90% of the state average.
items: Wait 7: no weekly comp is paid unless the incapacity lasts at least 1 week
Day 8: pay starts; at 2 weeks or longer, it's computed from the date of injury
80% of the after-tax average weekly wage for total disability
Cap: 90% of the state average weekly wage, set each January 1

draw.text: Off 2 weeks or more: from the injury date
$1,000 a week after taxes: comp pays $800

beats.text: Marco's laid up. In Michigan, the hook: wait 7, paid from day 8, back-paid at 2 weeks. Then 80% of after-tax wages, capped at 90% of the state average.
beats.say: Marco's laid up. In Michigan, the hook: wait seven, paid from day eight, back-paid at two weeks. Then eighty percent of after-tax wages, capped at ninety percent of the state average.

beats.text: Wait 7 is the waiting period: no weekly comp is paid unless he's off at least a week. Off 2 weeks or longer? Pay is computed from the date of injury.
beats.say: Wait seven is the waiting period: no weekly comp is paid unless he's off at least a week. Off two weeks or longer? Pay is computed from the date of injury.

beats.text: The 80% is of the after-tax average weekly wage, for total disability. Earn $1,000 a week after taxes, and comp pays $800. Watch out: 90% is the cap, not the benefit.
beats.say: The eighty percent is of the after-tax average weekly wage, for total disability. Earn one thousand dollars a week after taxes, and comp pays eight hundred dollars. Watch out: ninety percent is the cap, not the benefit.

beats.text: The cap is 90% of the state average weekly wage, set each January 1.
beats.say: The cap is ninety percent of the state average weekly wage, set each January first.

scenes.q: Marco can't work for 3 weeks after his fall. Under Michigan's act, his weekly comp is:
choices: Computed from the date of injury
Paid starting on the 8th day only
Paid starting on the 15th day only
Not paid for the first week
scenes.why: If the incapacity lasts 2 weeks or longer, compensation is computed from the date of injury. Day 8 is the start only when he is out more than 1 week but less than 2.

beats.text: Quick check: Marco can't work for 3 weeks. How is his weekly comp paid? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Quick check: Marco can't work for three weeks. How is his weekly comp paid? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: From the date of injury. At 2 weeks or longer, even the first week gets paid.
reveal.say: From the date of injury. At two weeks or longer, even the first week gets paid.

scenes.title: Rails, shore, ship: Tony's riverfront lunch run

draw.text: Sue for damages: prove the railroad's negligence
No-fault: navigable waters, piers, wharves, dry docks
Crew sue the employer, with a jury

beats.text: Tony delivers lunch to workers under three federal laws, outside Michigan's act.
beats.say: Tony delivers lunch to workers under three federal laws, outside Michigan's act.

beats.text: Rails: under FELA, the Federal Employers' Liability Act, interstate railroad workers sue for damages, proving the railroad's negligence. Their own negligence only reduces the award.
beats.say: Rails: under F E L A, the Federal Employers' Liability Act, interstate railroad workers sue for damages, proving the railroad's negligence. Their own negligence only reduces the award.

beats.text: Shore: the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, or USL&HW. It pays no-fault benefits to workers like ship repairers, on navigable waters, piers, wharves and dry docks.
beats.say: Shore: the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, or U S L and H W. It pays no-fault benefits to workers like ship repairers, on navigable waters, piers, wharves and dry docks.

beats.text: Ship: under the Jones Act, a crew member sues the employer with a jury trial. All three groups' employers need endorsements: the standard comp policy excludes all three.
beats.say: Ship: under the Jones Act, a crew member sues the employer with a jury trial. All three groups' employers need endorsements: the standard comp policy excludes all three.

scenes.title: Gino's call: which law?
scenes.src: 46 USC 30104(a); 33 USC 902(3)(G); 45 USC 51; questions core-063, core-wcg-07; table vs_commercial-07

draw.text: I'm part of the crew. Now what?

beats.text: Tony's cousin Gino cooks on a Great Lakes freighter. He's hurt aboard through the company's negligence.
beats.say: Tony's cousin Gino cooks on a Great Lakes freighter. He's hurt aboard through the company's negligence.

beats.text: I'm part of the crew. Now what?
beats.say: I'm part of the crew. Now what?
beats.speaker: Gino

options.label: Claim Longshore Act benefits
options.fail: The Longshore Act excludes a master or member of a crew of any vessel. A ship's crew goes to the Jones Act.

beats.text: Denied. The Longshore Act excludes a vessel's crew, and Gino is crew.
beats.say: Denied. The Longshore Act excludes a vessel's crew, and Gino is crew.

options.label: Sue the shipping company under FELA
options.fail: FELA itself covers interstate railroad workers. Gino's suit goes under the Jones Act, which borrows FELA's rules.

beats.text: Wrong track, literally. FELA itself is for railroad workers.
beats.say: Wrong track, literally. F E L A itself is for railroad workers.

draw.text: But I work on a ship...

options.label: Sue his employer under the Jones Act
options.win: A seaman, a vessel's crew member, sues the employer under the Jones Act, with a jury trial. FELA's rules apply.

beats.text: Right. As crew, Gino sues his employer under the Jones Act, before a jury.
beats.say: Right. As crew, Gino sues his employer under the Jones Act, before a jury.

reveal.text: Railroad worker: FELA. Dock or shipyard worker: Longshore Act, which excludes crew. Ship's crew: Jones Act.
reveal.say: Railroad worker: F E L A. Dock or shipyard worker: Longshore Act, which excludes crew. Ship's crew: Jones Act.

scenes.title: Tony's policy: the six C's
scenes.src: NCCI WC 00 00 00 C (Ed. 1-15), Parts One-Six; MCL 418.621(4)(g); WC 21 03 04; mn_core-29; cp_commercial-15

spots.label: Part One: Comp
spots.text: Pays the benefits Michigan's comp law requires. There is no dollar limit: the law sets the benefits.

spots.label: Part Two: Court
spots.text: Employers liability: damages when Tony is sued over a worker's injury where law allows, like a third-party-over suit. Not injury he causes on purpose. Limits: Item 3.B.

spots.label: Part Three: Crossing state lines
spots.text: Other states insurance: applies only to states listed in Item 3.C.

spots.label: Part Four: Call us at once
spots.text: After an injury, tell the insurer at once, and provide the immediate medical care the law requires.

spots.label: Part Five: Cash
spots.text: The premium shown is only an estimate. An audit of the actual exposure, usually payroll, sets the final premium.

spots.label: Part Six: Conditions
spots.text: The insurer cancels with at least 10 days' notice. In Michigan, it also files notice with the state comp agency at least 20 days before.

beats.text: Here's your policy, Tony: six parts, six C's. Comp, court, crossing state lines, call us at once, cash, and conditions.
beats.say: Here's your policy, Tony: six parts, six C's. Comp, court, crossing state lines, call us at once, cash, and conditions.

beats.text: Tap each glowing picture.
beats.say: Tap each glowing picture.

reveal.text: Part One has no dollar limit; Part Two has limits. The premium is an estimate until the audit.
reveal.say: Part One has no dollar limit; Part Two has limits. The premium is an estimate until the audit.

reveal.text: The insurer cancels on at least 10 days' notice. In Michigan, it also files with the agency at least 20 days ahead.
reveal.say: The insurer cancels on at least ten days' notice. In Michigan, it also files with the agency at least twenty days ahead.

scenes.title: Figuring Tony's premium
scenes.src: NCRB Basic Manual Rule 5; IRMI: manual and standard premium, experience mod, premium discount; question core-066

goal.text: Find the payroll that makes Tony's premium $8,500 after the mod.

draw.text: A 1.25 mod would be a debit: it raises the premium

beats.text: Rates are per $100 of payroll. Payroll divided by 100, times the rate, is the manual premium. Tony's rate is $4 per $100 of payroll.
beats.say: Rates are per one hundred dollars of payroll. Payroll divided by one hundred, times the rate, is the manual premium. Tony's rate is four dollars per one hundred dollars of payroll.

beats.text: The experience mod compares Tony's own losses with expected losses: under 1 is a credit, over 1 a debit. Tony's mod is 0.85, a credit. A 1.25 mod would be a debit: it raises the premium.
beats.say: The experience mod compares Tony's own losses with expected losses: under one is a credit, over one a debit. Tony's mod is zero point eight five, a credit. A one point two five mod would be a debit: it raises the premium.

beats.text: Your turn: find the payroll that makes Tony's premium $8,500 after the mod.
beats.say: Your turn: find the payroll that makes Tony's premium eight thousand five hundred dollars after the mod.

reveal.text: $250,000. That's $10,000 of manual premium, times 0.85: $8,500, the standard premium.
reveal.say: Two hundred fifty thousand dollars. That's ten thousand dollars of manual premium, times zero point eight five: eight thousand five hundred dollars, the standard premium.

reveal.text: A premium discount for larger policies comes after the mod.
reveal.say: A premium discount for larger policies comes after the mod.

scenes.q: Down the street, a bakery's payroll is $100,000, its rate is $5 per $100 of payroll, and its experience mod is 1.25. What is its premium after the mod?
scenes.why: $100,000 divided by 100 is 1,000. Times $5 is $5,000 manual premium. A 1.25 mod is a debit: $5,000 times 1.25 is $6,250. $5,000 forgets the mod; $3,750 treats it as a credit.

beats.text: Now you do the math. Pick an answer.
beats.say: Now you do the math. Pick an answer.

reveal.text: $6,250: $5,000 of manual premium, times the 1.25 debit.
reveal.say: Six thousand two hundred fifty dollars: five thousand dollars of manual premium, times the one point two five debit.

reveal.text: $100,000 divided by 100 is 1,000, times $5 is $5,000. $5,000 forgets the mod; $3,750 treats the debit as a credit.
reveal.say: One hundred thousand dollars divided by one hundred is one thousand, times five dollars is five thousand dollars. Five thousand dollars forgets the mod; three thousand seven hundred fifty dollars treats the debit as a credit.

items: Must carry: 3 at once, or 1 at 35 for 13 of 52; all public employers
Comp is the exclusive remedy; only an intentional tort escapes it
Paid from day 8; from the injury date at 2 weeks; 80% after-tax AWW
Rails: FELA. Shore: Longshore Act. Ship's crew: Jones Act

beats.text: What a Friday! Who must carry comp? 3 at once, or 1 at 35 for 13 of the last 52, plus all public employers. Comp is the exclusive remedy, and only an intentional tort opens the trapdoor.
beats.say: What a Friday! Who must carry comp? Three at once, or one at thirty-five for thirteen of the last fifty-two, plus all public employers. Comp is the exclusive remedy, and only an intentional tort opens the trapdoor.

beats.text: Paid from day 8, or the injury date at 2 weeks, at 80% of after-tax average weekly wage. Rails: FELA. Shore: Longshore Act. Ship's crew: Jones Act. Premium: payroll divided by 100, times rate, times experience mod.
beats.say: Paid from day eight, or the injury date at two weeks, at eighty percent of after-tax average weekly wage. Rails: F E L A. Shore: Longshore Act. Ship's crew: Jones Act. Premium: payroll divided by one hundred, times rate, times experience mod.

beats.text: And yes, I bought the floor mat.
beats.say: And yes, I bought the floor mat.
